In 1.5°C pathways, net zero CO2 emissions occur earlier than net zero GHG emissions. This is because limiting human-caused global warming to a specific level requires reaching net zero or net negative CO2 emissions, alongside strong reductions in other GHG emissions, whereas achieving net zero GHG emissions requires all remaining CO2 and metric-weighted non-CO2 GHG emissions to reach zero.

The quantification of net zero GHG emissions is determined by two choices:
1. The GHG emission metric chosen to compare emissions and removals of different gases (e.g., global warming potential over a 100-year period) [chunk_id: 143].
2. The time horizon chosen for that metric [chunk_id: 143]. [ipcc-ar6-syr-2023:p143:text:c001]

Section 3 of the IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report assesses the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) over the 21st century as follows:

*   **Weakening:** It is very likely that the AMOC will weaken over the 21st century for all considered scenarios (high confidence) [p. 94].
*   **Abrupt Collapse:** There is medium confidence that the AMOC will not collapse abruptly before 2100 [p. 34, p. 94].
*   **Impacts of Collapse:** If an abrupt collapse were to occur, it would very likely cause abrupt shifts in regional weather patterns and the water cycle (such as a southward shift in the tropical rain belt), as well as large impacts on ecosystems and human activities [p. 34, p. 94].
